extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic, philosophy of science, and mathematics seeking an account of syllogism and inference
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and evaluate the nature, structure, and logical value of syllogisms and their relation to induction; includes canonical forms (figures and moods), reduction rules, and philosophical critique of deductive practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential structure of a legitimate syllogism
rubrics_metrics.description: To a legitimate syllogism it is essential that there should be three, and no more than three, propositions (the conclusion and two premises), and three, and no more than three, terms (the subject and predicate of the conclusion, and a middle term found in both premises). The premise containing the middle and major term is the major premise; that with the middle and minor term is the minor premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This entry specifies the minimal formal requirements for constructing a valid syllogism. Check that exactly two premises are used, exactly three distinct terms appear, and the middle term occurs in both premises (not in the conclusion). Failure to meet these counts or placements invalidates the syllogistic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by figures (position of the middle term)
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogisms are divided into figures according to the position of the middle term: (1) middle term subject of major and predicate of minor (first figure, most common); (2) middle term predicate in both premises (second figure); (3) middle term subject in both (third figure); (4) middle term subject of minor and predicate of major (fourth figure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or formulating a syllogism, identify the figure by locating the middle term in each premise. Some authors compress figures (three-figure vs four-figure systems); note that any syllogism in figures 2–4 can be reduced to the first figure (see reduction rules). Consider which figure best displays the argument's naturalness; an argument may be clearer in a non-first figure even if reducible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division into moods (quantity and quality of propositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each figure is divided into moods according to the quantity (universal/particular) and quality (affirmative/negative) of the propositions. Only certain combinations (moods) are legitimate — the work lists the canonical legitimate moods for the first through fourth figures with explicit blank forms (e.g., All B is C; All A is B; therefore All A is C, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate a syllogism by checking that its combination of universal/particular and affirmative/negative premises matches one of the legitimate moods for its figure. Use the provided exemplar forms as templates. Singular propositions are to be treated with universals for mood-classification purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to first figure (rules for conversion and per accidens)
rubrics_metrics.description: All correct ratiocination admits of being stated in syllogisms of the first figure alone. Arguments in other figures can be reduced by converting one or both premises (simple conversion for universal negatives; conversion per accidens for universal affirmatives to particulars), yielding an equivalent first-figure form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing validity, attempt to reduce a given syllogism to the first figure: apply simple conversion (e.g., No C is B → No B is C) or conversion per accidens (All B is A → Some A is B) where appropriate. Successful reduction demonstrating an equivalent first-figure syllogism supports legitimacy. Note: reduction may alter surface language but preserves the proof-contributing content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of singular propositions in syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Singular propositions are not given separate place in the blank forms; they are ranked, for syllogistic purposes, with universal propositions because their predicate is affirmed or denied of the whole of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a premise names an individual (e.g., 'Socrates is a man'), treat it as if universal in mood-classification and in reduction so that standard syllogistic rules apply. This allows direct mapping to canonical moods and figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roles of major and minor premises (major must be universal; minor affirmative)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the general formulæ both have one premise (the major) universal, and the other premise always affirmative, asserting inclusion of the minor term (individual/class/part) in the class named in the major premise. The conclusion mirrors the major premise's generality (affirmative/negative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the major premise provides a general claim about a class (universal) and that the minor premise affirms membership in that class. The form determines whether the conclusion will be universal/particular and affirmative/negative. Violations suggest incorrect syllogistic setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions must assert factual content, not mere verbal conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every proposition which conveys real information asserts a matter of fact dependent on laws of nature, not mere classification or the meaning of words. Syllogistic analysis that treats propositions purely as class-relations (as Hobbes did) is insufficient to account for real ratiocination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate premises for substantive factual import: do they claim co-occurrence or laws about attributes in the world, or are they merely definitional/linguistic? Arguments grounded only in the latter may amount to tautology and not genuine inference. Favor formulations that reflect facts about attributes and their co-existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental factual axioms underlying syllogistic legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The true principles of syllogistic legitimacy are factual axioms: (affirmative) 'things which co-exist with the same thing, co-exist with one another' (i.e., transitivity of co-existence of attributes); (negative) 'a thing which co-exists with another thing, with which other a third thing does not co-exist, is not co-existent with that third thing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether a syllogism legitimately yields its conclusion, reference these factual axioms: ensure the premises claim co-existence relations between attributes such that transitivity (or its negative analogue) justifies the conclusion. This grounds syllogistic validity in facts rather than mere naming conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogism-as-mark formulation (practical/epistemic reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every syllogism can be recast: 'Attribute A is a mark of attribute B; the given object has the mark A; therefore the given object has attribute B.' This interprets universals as practical evidential marks rather than metaphysical universals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'mark' formulation to assess syllogisms as instruments for inference in practice: does the major premise justify taking A as reliable evidence (a mark) for B? Is the minor premise establishing that the object has that mark? This reading clarifies the syllogism's epistemic function in producing belief about particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of syllogistic inference (petitio principii) and its epistemic role
rubrics_metrics.description: A syllogism is vicious if there is anything in the conclusion not already assumed in the premises — nothing can be proved by syllogism that was not, in some sense, already in the premises. Nonetheless, syllogisms frequently bring to light truths that are new to a particular reasoner by unfolding what was implicit in the premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using or evaluating syllogisms, be explicit about what content is assumed vs what is merely made explicit. Recognize that syllogisms do not create empirical knowledge beyond their premises; their value lies in clarifying implicit consequences and enabling practical inference from general principles to unobserved particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise definition of 'induction' and 'ratiocination' by generality shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction: inferring a proposition from propositions less general than itself (conclusion more general than premises). Ratiocination (syllogism): inferring a proposition from propositions equally or more general (conclusion equally or less general than largest premise, or particular/individual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these definitions rather than loose 'from particulars to generals' wording. When classifying an argument as inductive or ratiocinative, check whether the conclusion increases generality relative to premises (induction) or reduces/maintains it (ratiocination). This precision avoids conceptual confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical ordering: treat ratiocination before induction when tracing sources of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Though experience proceeds from individuals to generals, it is advantageous in a science that traces acquired knowledge to its sources to commence with ratiocination (deduction), tracing derivative truths back to the truths from which they are deduced before pointing out the original spring (induction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting or learning logical theory and the sources of knowledge, consider beginning with analysis of deductive dependencies (how derivative truths follow from principles) to clarify evidential chains before addressing how general principles themselves are established by induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction is a real inference with broader conclusion than premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is a process of real inference: the conclusion in an induction embraces more than is contained in the premises — a general principle ascertained by experience covers a much larger extent than individual experiments upon which it is grounded and supports belief about unobserved or future cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing inductive reasoning, verify that the generalization legitimately extends beyond observed instances and consider the conditions required to make such an inference legitimate (not detailed here but noted as necessary). Distinguish legitimate generalization from mere summation of observed cases.
